subject.title: Convalescent (aka Petit Dejeuner; note in opal)
subject.author: James McNeill Whistler

title: He Kept His Own Wedding Secret Just to Keep Her Away From It
standfirst: James McNeill Whistler titled this 1884 watercolour after an illness, not a name. The woman in it was Maud Franklin, his primary model and, in practice if never in law, his wife of over a decade — a role Whistler ended four years later by marrying someone else in a ceremony kept deliberately hidden from her.

sections.heading: A Word for What He Wouldn't Name
sections.body: Whistler spent the 1870s and after re-titling his own work in the vocabulary of music rather than portraiture — a *nocturne*, a *symphony*, a *harmony*, an *arrangement* — deliberately steering attention away from who or what a picture actually showed. This one follows the pattern exactly: catalogued at its first showing as *Petit Déjeuner; note in opal*, and known today as *Convalescent*, it is named for a mood and a state of health, not a person. The University of Glasgow's catalogue of Whistler's paintings identifies the sitter anyway: Maud Franklin, 1857 to 1939, watercolour on paper, roughly 245 by 171 millimetres. Whistler's own title tells the viewer she was unwell. It does not tell them who she was.

sections.heading: The Fifteen-Year-Old Who Stood In for Someone's Wife
sections.body: Franklin may have first posed for Whistler as early as 1872, at fifteen, standing in for Frances Leyland while he worked on her portrait. By the late 1870s she had become his regular model for etchings and painted portraits, sitting for, among others, *Arrangement in White and Black*, the *Portrait of Miss Florence Leyland*, and *Harmony in Grey and Peach Colour*, alongside dozens of drawings, watercolours and lithographs that carry no name in their titles at all. Almost everything documented about her in this period exists because Whistler painted it. She left comparatively little record of her own from these years — not because there wasn't one, but because the one that survives is mostly his.

sections.heading: What 1884 Actually Followed
sections.body: The libel trial Whistler brought against the critic John Ruskin in 1878 won him a verdict and a farthing in damages, with court costs split between them — a result that ruined him anyway. The costs, on top of debts from building his Tite Street studio-house, bankrupted him by May 1879, and his work, collections and the house itself went to auction. He left for Venice on a three-month etching commission that stretched to fourteen, arriving with Franklin at his side; the run of etchings, nocturnes and pastels he brought back began paying his debts down. By May 1884 he was showing new work at Messrs Dowdeswell's gallery in London under the title *Notes — Harmonies — Nocturnes*, this watercolour among them as catalogue number 13. The *Daily News* reviewed it in one line: "A fine frowsiness is delicately conveyed."

sections.heading: Mrs. Whistler, Unofficially
sections.body: By her own account and his circle's, Franklin called herself Mrs. Whistler; Whistler, in company, called her Madame. She bore him two daughters, Ione, born around 1877, and Maud McNeill Whistler Franklin, born in 1879. None of it was formalised. For more than a decade she filled the position of a wife through a bankruptcy, an exile in Venice, and the exhibition that rebuilt his reputation and income, without the legal standing, name or public acknowledgment that would have come with the word actually being true.

sections.heading: The Wedding Built to Exclude Her
sections.body: The architect Edward William Godwin, who had designed Whistler's Tite Street house and lost the commission to Whistler's bankruptcy before he ever moved in, died in 1886. Two years later Whistler married Godwin's widow, Beatrice, on 11 August 1888, in a ceremony arranged hastily at the urging of mutual friends and attended by a reporter from the *Pall Mall Gazette* but almost no one else — a secrecy later accounts trace directly to keeping a furious Maud Franklin from interrupting it. Franklin left for Paris afterward.

sections.heading: What Outlasted the Title
sections.body: In Paris, and for years before under the name Clifton Lin, Franklin exhibited her own paintings at the Grosvenor Gallery — work made alongside, not just in front of, the pictures for which she is now chiefly remembered. She later married an American, John A. Little, until his death in 1904, then Richard H. S. Abbott around 1911, and lived near Cannes until she died in 1939, outliving Whistler by thirty-six years. What remains of the years she spent as the uncredited centre of his household is scattered across dozens of works like this one: catalogued, dated, occasionally reviewed in a single dry sentence, and titled for almost anything except her.
